title: India and Canada Just Agreed to Triple Their Trade to $50 Billion. The Largest-Ever Indian Delegation Flew to Ottawa to Seal It.
excerpt: Piyush Goyal led 112 Indian companies to Canada for CEPA negotiations, a trade forum launch, and a handshake with Mark Carney. For 1.8 million Indian-Canadians, the thaw could not come sooner.
body:
India and Canada launched the Canada-India Trade and Investment Forum last week, formally resetting a bilateral relationship that had been in cold storage for years. Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal flew to Ottawa and Toronto with representatives from over 112 Indian companies — the largest business delegation India has ever sent abroad.

The numbers tell the story of a relationship that has been punching below its weight. Bilateral trade currently stands at about $8.5 billion, a figure both governments now consider embarrassingly low. The new target is $50 billion by 2030 — roughly a sixfold increase — with a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) expected to be signed before the end of this year.

What Changed

The inflection point was Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to India earlier this year. Carney, who took office promising to rebuild Canada's fraying international partnerships, signalled a clear departure from the diplomatic freeze that had defined the Trudeau era. The two prime ministers agreed on a terms of reference for CEPA in March, and negotiations have moved at unusual speed since.

"When it comes to working together for the shared prosperity of the people of India, the people of Canada, the speed and intent of both sides is phenomenal," Goyal said at a joint press conference with Canadian Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu. He described the $50 billion target as "very much doable," citing the trust between Modi and Carney as the driving force.

What Is on the Table

The talks cover a wide canvas: market access for goods, customs and trade facilitation, non-tariff barriers, investment promotion, and what both sides are calling "economic security alignment." The sectors identified for deepened cooperation include clean energy, critical minerals, agri-food, advanced manufacturing, AI research, semiconductors, and digital infrastructure.

Goyal also met Canada's Foreign Minister Anita Anand and Agriculture Minister Heath MacDonald. Discussions with institutional investors — including Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan and CPP Investments — focused on Indian infrastructure, renewables, logistics, and digital economy opportunities.

Sidhu confirmed that Canada will send a "Team Canada Trade Mission" to India in November, bringing Canadian firms looking to expand in the Indian market.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the 1.8 million people of Indian origin in Canada — one of the largest diaspora communities in any Western nation — the trade reset carries significance that goes beyond economics. The relationship between New Delhi and Ottawa had deteriorated sharply under Justin Trudeau, with allegations and counter-allegations that strained consular services, student visa processing, and community engagement.

Goyal acknowledged this explicitly, praising the "invaluable contribution of the Indo-Canadian community in bringing the two nations closer through stronger business engagement and people-to-people ties." The CEPA framework includes provisions for improved business mobility — a signal that the human side of the relationship is part of the negotiation, not an afterthought.

The Road Ahead

The ambition is clear, but the path is narrow. Canada's own trade agenda is crowded: it is simultaneously navigating tensions with China, renegotiating aspects of CUSMA with the United States, and managing domestic political pressure on immigration. India, for its part, is juggling trade negotiations with the US, the EU, and the UK, all at various stages of completion.

The CEPA deadline of year-end 2026 is aggressive by any standard. India's track record on free trade agreements — the Australia deal took years, the UK deal remains unsigned — suggests that political will alone may not be enough. But the signals from both capitals are unusually aligned, and the business community on both sides appears to be pushing rather than waiting.

For Indian-Canadians who weathered the diplomatic chill, the turnaround feels overdue. Whether the numbers follow the rhetoric will be the test of the next six months.

Sources: Ministry of Commerce and Industry press releases; Reuters; The Indian Eye
